description: Atlas é a equipe sergipana de inteligência territorial que desenvolve tecnologia para transformar dados, projetos e iniciativas em impacto real.
summary: SpaceAtlas: Mission Control is a free browser game that puts players in charge of a real space mission, from the first requirement to the final debrief. Players sign a mission contract, choose a target (Earth observation, the Moon's south pole, a real near-Earth asteroid or Mars), design the spacecraft and its science payload, pick the orbit and the rocket, and balance cost, mass, power, data and lifetime. Every choice is explained in plain words and checked with the same first-order rules engineers use in early studies. The mission is then flown in 3D, with events driven by real NASA data such as space weather and asteroid close approaches. The debrief traces every lost point to a number, compares the design with hundreds of other valid spacecraft, and lets players rerun the mission changing one decision. It runs on phones and desktops, in English, Portuguese and Spanish, solo or with up to four players.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

SpaceAtlas turns the full mission-design loop into a 10-minute game:

1. Contract: the player sets the minimum and full success goals the mission will be judged against.

2. Design: ten guided questions (objective, duration, instruments, orbit, size, power, battery, propulsion, communications, rocket). Each answer shows the numbers it changed. Secondary decisions (thermal, computer, redundancy, shielding, radio band, ground network) are settled automatically, and a hint shows the smallest change that fixes a failing check.

3. Go/No-Go: every budget (mass, power, energy, data, delta-v, cost, margins) is checked before launch.

4. Flight: a cinematic 3D launch and mission. Two or three events arrive (13 kinds, such as coronal mass ejections, a stuck solar wing, micrometeoroids, debris conjunctions, budget cuts or an unexpected discovery), and the player decides how to respond. The outcome depends on the design and on the decision.

5. Board of Investigation: the verdict against the player's own goals, a waterfall of where the science came from, a comparison with 100–400 other valid designs (value for money as distance to the science-versus-cost Pareto frontier), and a one-change rerun that keeps the same random seed, so the comparison is fair.

The physics engine is deterministic and separate from the interface. It includes the rocket equation (Tsiolkovsky), solar power falling with distance squared plus cell degradation and eclipse or night fractions, battery depth of discharge against the longest dark period, radioisotope power with decay, a simplified link budget (data rate falls with distance squared; data per day = rate × contact time), and design margins of 10, 15 or 20 % by difficulty, following ESA's margin philosophy for early studies.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Mission design is usually taught as isolated formulas. SpaceAtlas shows how every decision pulls on every other one: a bigger camera needs more power, which needs bigger solar panels, which adds mass, which needs a bigger rocket and a bigger budget. It targets high-school and early university students, and the general public. It is free, needs no install or account, and works on low-end phones and in three languages, so it can be used in classrooms with few resources. Because the debrief explains failures with numbers instead of a score alone, players learn why engineers keep margins, why Mars missions need larger solar panels, and why a light-delay of minutes requires autonomy. The team mode (Systems & Budget, Spacecraft, Science, Comms & Ops) reproduces the trade-offs between subsystems that real mission teams negotiate.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE

- Languages: TypeScript, Python (asset build scripts), Node.js scripts.

- Interface: Preact, Vite, three.js (3D scenes, launch films, an exploded view of spacecraft and rocket parts), sounds synthesised in the browser with the Web Audio API.

- Quality: Vitest (physics, sizing model, simulation, translations with identical keys), Playwright with Chromium (end-to-end play-through of every mission, screenshots at 390 px and 1440 px, performance measurements).

- Data: NASA open APIs (DONKI, NeoWs, EONET), JPL CNEOS NHATS and the Close-Approach Data API, NASA SVS and NASA 3D Resources.

- Hosting: Vercel (static web build); the same build also runs as a one-file page.

- Trailer: Remotion (React video), FFmpeg (mix and loudness), Kokoro-82M text-to-speech for the narration.

- Hardware: no special hardware; it runs in any modern browser.

CREATIVITY

The game uses mission-control roles instead of a sandbox: players sign a contract and are later judged by it. Space weather is shown as it is really observed (flare, particle tracks on the camera sensor, the plasma cloud, aurora), not as explosions. Every spacecraft and rocket part can be tapped for a plain-language explanation, and "Separate parts" opens an exploded view of the stages, boosters and fairing. The four playable crew members are fictional pixel-art characters whose paths are inspired by real NASA astronauts.

FACTORS THE TEAM CONSIDERED

- Scientific honesty: first-order models, clearly labelled as for learning trade-offs, not for flight; every constant has a cited source; no purely random failures, so outcomes always come from the design and the decisions.

- Fairness: a shared seed for the whole team, and reruns that keep the seed.

- Accessibility: keyboard navigation, visible focus, a reduced-motion setting, mute, readable contrast, responsive layouts for phones and desktops, and quality tiers that adapt to weaker devices.

- Reach: three languages, no account, small first download (about 0.7 MB), and an offline data snapshot when live APIs cannot be reached.

- Brand rules: no NASA logos or insignia are used, and the game states that NASA does not endorse it.
